> AVA is a mobile AI robot powered by Hermes Agent. It combines a touchscreen, cameras, speakers, sensors, motors, and a custom electronics system inside a 3D-printed enclosure. Hermes acts as the robot's intelligent agent, while AVA provides the physical body and hardware interface, allowing the AI to perceive its environment, communicate with users, and control the robot's movement and peripherals.

![pic2](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/R7nIII549ICPnqm2m1FpXVoeyFfOb41u/1911d1dfce0a1410630161135a572fd6c99f89bba367f54b8920168364795558.png)

I started by figuring out what I wanted AVA-ROBOT to be and what it would need inside. The idea is a compact AI companion with a screen and a wheeled body. Before modelling the parts, I thought through the main components—the onboard computer, battery, display, and drive hardware—and how they could fit together.

From there, I moved into CAD and started designing the parts. I worked on the body and chassis, the wheel arrangement, and the internal space for the electronics. I went back and forth between the outside shape and the inside layout rather than treating them as separate designs. Understanding the build and making this first version took around three hours.

I then spent another 30 minutes refining that version. I checked the model from different angles and adjusted how the parts fitted together. The three images show the underside and connector access, the computer mounted inside the torso, and a cutaway showing the battery and other internal components.

With that layout in place, I spent the final hour planning the PCB and how the electronics would connect. I considered what the custom board needs to do, which components need to communicate, and how power should be supplied. I haven’t completed the schematic or routed the PCB yet—this stage was about defining the requirements before starting the board design.

Next, I’ll confirm the components and their electrical requirements, turn the connection plan into a schematic, and build the bill of materials. I’ll also check the PCB outline and connector positions against the enclosure.

Total time: 4 hours 30 minutes.

### 2026-10-09 – This session focused on planning the camera connection for AVA-ROBOT. With AI assistance, I examined Raspberry Pi’s published Compute Module 5 IO Board design in KiCad and identified its two camera/di

**4.5h**

This session focused on planning the camera connection for AVA-ROBOT. With AI assistance, I examined Raspberry Pi’s published Compute Module 5 IO Board design in KiCad and identified its two camera/display connectors. I chose J5 / CAM-DISP 0 as the proposed camera port and prepared layout images and a short video walkthrough. The camera routing already existed, so I kept it unchanged rather than redesigning it. Next I need to select a compatible camera and ribbon cable, then configure and test the hardware.

### 2026-10-09 – I spent this session comparing the Raspberry Pi 5 with the D-Robotics RDK S100P for AVA. I focused on camera support, onboard AI and robot control. With AI assistance, I checked the official specifica

**4h**

I spent this session comparing the Raspberry Pi 5 with the D-Robotics RDK S100P for AVA. I focused on camera support, onboard AI and robot control. With AI assistance, I checked the official specifications and how each board would affect the build. The Pi 5 looks like the simpler starting point, while the S100P offers dedicated AI acceleration and robot-control hardware. I still need to test whether my models run well on it—its advertised 128 TOPS doesn’t tell me the actual performance of my application. I also clarified that the CM5 IO Board design from my previous entry is a separate reference and cannot be reused as an S100P carrier. This session was research and planning, not hardware testing.
